title: The Three-Month Forecast Trap: What Your First Quarter Profit Number Actually Tells You
linkedin:
Three months of FY27 are done. The obvious next move is to take the quarter's profit, multiply by four, and call it the year's number.

That number will be confident. It will also be wrong, in a specific and predictable way.

Here's what actually sits inside a July to September quarter that a full twelve months would smooth out. A 1 July price rise usually takes six to eight weeks to fully flow through invoiced revenue, so September understates where pricing lands by December. A new hire brought on in August carries a full quarter of cost against only a partial quarter of the revenue they were meant to generate. June's EOFY write-offs and provisions sit in last year's numbers, not this one, which flatters the new quarter by comparison.

None of this makes the Q1 number wrong. It makes it a narrower answer than the question most owners are asking of it.

What a first quarter is genuinely good for is testing whether your FY27 budget assumptions are holding up, not replacing the forecast altogether. The businesses that read this moment well feed the quarter's actuals back into a rolling model and adjust what turned out to be wrong, rather than multiplying a snapshot into a verdict.

Three months of the new financial year are in the books, and it's tempting to take that quarter's profit, times it by four, and call it your year.

Worth pausing on that one. A July to September quarter carries its own quirks: price rises that haven't fully landed yet, new hires costing more than they're producing so far, and June's EOFY write-offs no longer dragging the number down. Multiply all that by four and you've just made a small quarterly distortion into a full-year one.

Have you actually gone back and checked your Q1 numbers against what you budgeted back in June, or is the spreadsheet still sitting exactly as it was set on 1 July?

Three months into the new financial year, a lot of business owners across Brisbane and the East Coast are doing the same thing with their numbers: taking the first quarter's profit, multiplying by four, and treating that as the year's forecast.

It's an understandable shortcut, but a July to September quarter rarely represents a fair sample of the full twelve months. Price increases from 1 July often take a couple of months to fully show up in revenue, new staff can cost more than they're generating in their first few months, and last financial year's EOFY costs are no longer in the picture to weigh the number down. All of that can make an early quarter look either better or worse than the year will actually turn out.

The better use of a first quarter is checking whether the assumptions in your original budget are holding up, then feeding what you learn back into a proper twelve-month forecast rather than a single multiplied number.

If you built your FY27 budget in a hurry at the end of June, now is a good time to revisit it properly. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
